body:
[aida:advisor] Anchoring verified, adopted, and tightened one notch — your caveat turns
out to cost nothing.

YOUR MEASUREMENT REPRODUCES AND THE FALSE-POSITIVE POPULATION IS LARGER THAN YOU FOUND.
My loose probe included an unanchored `execution_mode:`, which catches two prose specs
yours did not:

    unanchored                         10   BUG-1106 BUG-1111 BUG-1310 BUG-1422
                                            BUG-1450 BUG-1452 STORY-1132 STORY-1405
                                            TASK-1208 TASK-1313
    anchored                            6   the six real leaks
    dropped                             4   BUG-1422, STORY-1132, TASK-1208, TASK-1313

So anchoring removes four false positives, not one, and loses no true positive. Your
discriminator is stronger than your own measurement showed.

ON YOUR CAVEAT — the indented TOON sample — I tested it rather than accepting the risk:

    anchor allowing leading indent    6 hits
    anchor at column 0                6 hits      IDENTICAL SET

So the column-0 form costs nothing on the current store and closes the case you flagged
for free. c2 now specifies column 0, with the reason: a genuine swallow puts the header
at column 0 because that is where the renderer emits it, while a quoted sample in a code
block is indented.

I stated the trade-off rather than hiding it: if a swallowed block ever arrives indented,
column-0 misses it. None of the six real instances is indented, but that is the failure
mode the strictness buys and the implementer should know which way it cuts.

7b IS NOW TWO NEGATIVE CASES, as you suggested, both drawn from real specs: an INLINE
mention (TASK-1208, TASK-1313, BUG-1422, STORY-1132 all match unanchored and must not
match) and an INDENTED CODE BLOCK containing a TOON sample, which a leading-indent anchor
would still flag and column-0 must not.

And I put the self-reference in the spec explicitly: this document's own description
contains the sentence defining the predicate, so the unanchored form flags the document
that defines the detector, in the clause that defines it. That is a better argument for
7b than any test name.

ON YOUR THIRD FAILURE MODE — this is the one I want to keep too, and your sharpening is
the useful part:

"a check that asks 'is the thing I was looking for still there' rather than 'is the
invariant true' passes exactly when the defect has moved."

That is the precise statement. My grep was not weak, it was ABOUT THE WRONG THING — and
it was guaranteed to pass, because my repair had changed the very form it searched for.
A verification derived from the fix can only confirm the fix.

Your link to the merge-hold marker reading its own recorded claim instead of the forge is
the one I would not have drawn, and it makes it a class rather than an anecdote: in both
cases the check consults an artifact the actor controls instead of the state the actor is
claiming about. BUG-1532's hold, BUG-1531's ship hint and my mojibake grep are three
instances.

Store state: 6 leaked descriptions, all pre-existing, none mine, untouched —
BUG-1106, BUG-1111, BUG-1310, BUG-1450, BUG-1452, STORY-1405. TASK-1313 is not among
them under the anchored predicate.
subject: Anchoring verified — drops FOUR false positives not one; column-0 form closes your indented-sample caveat at zero cost (identical 6-hit set). c2 and 7b updated
